record.text_content:
ARISTOTLE ON WISH AND THE APPEARANCE OF THE GOOD

This chapter addresses a fundamental question: Is the object of wish the real good or the apparent good? The answer has implications for moral responsibility.

, ' , ; ' , ..
, . ' , , .

 It has been said that wish is for the end, but some think it is for the good, others for the apparent good..
If these views are unsatisfactory, should we say that without qualification and in truth the object of wish is the good, but for each person it is the apparent good? For the virtuous person, then, it is what is truly so, but for the base person it is whatever happens to present itself..
For the virtuous person judges each thing correctly, and in each case what is true appears to him. For each state has its own special noble things and pleasant things, and perhaps the virtuous person differs most by seeing the truth in each case, being as it were a standard and measure of them.

Aristotle resolves the dilemma by distinguishing.
- Absolutely (ἁπλῶς): the real good is the object of wish
- For each person (ἑκάστῳ): the apparent good

The virtuous person (σπουδαῖος) serves as "standard and measure" (κανὼν καὶ μέτρον) - their character makes them see truly. This connects character formation to correct perception of the good.

Key concepts: wish (for the end/goal) (boulēsis); the good (tagathon); the apparent good (to phainomenon agathon); the virtuous/serious person (spoudaios); standard and measure (kanōn kai metron).

record.text_content:
ARISTOTLE'S FOUNDATIONAL ANALYSIS OF VOLUNTARY ACTION

This chapter establishes the criteria for moral responsibility that became the foundation for all subsequent ancient discussions of free will. Aristotle distinguishes voluntary (ἑκούσιον) from involuntary (ἀκούσιον) action to determine when praise and blame are appropriate.

 Since virtue is concerned with feelings and actions, and since praise and blame are given to what is voluntary while pardon, and sometimes pity, are given to what is involuntary, it is presumably necessary for those investigating virtue to define the voluntary and the involuntary; and it is also useful for legislators with regard to honors and punishments. Now it seems that things done by force or through ignorance are involuntary. What is forced has its origin outside, being the sort of thing in which the agent or patient contributes nothing..
Since what is involuntary is what is done by force or through ignorance, the voluntary would seem to be that of which the origin is in the agent himself, who knows the particular circumstances of the action.

This chapter establishes two criteria for voluntary action that became canonical.
1. The ORIGIN (ἀρχή) must be IN the agent (ἐν αὐτῷ)
2. The agent must have KNOWLEDGE (εἰδότι) of the particular circumstances

The concepts of (forced/compelled) and (ignorance) define the boundaries of moral responsibility.

Key concepts: voluntary - origin in agent with knowledge (hekousion); involuntary - by force or ignorance (akousion); forced - origin external, agent contributes nothing (biaion); origin, principle, starting-point (archē); ignorance of particulars (excusing) vs universal (culpable) (agnoia).

ARISTOTLE ON DELIBERATION AND THE SCOPE OF HUMAN AGENCY

This chapter defines the domain of deliberation and thereby the scope of ' (what is up to us) - the crucial concept for all subsequent free will debates.

' · ..
, , ..

 Do people deliberate about everything, and is everything an object of deliberation, or about some things is there no deliberation?... About eternal things no one deliberates, for instance about the cosmos or the incommensurability of the diagonal and side. Nor about things that are in motion but always happen in the same way, whether by necessity or by nature..
We deliberate about things that are up to us and are matters of action; and these are in fact what remain..

record.text_content:
ARISTOTLE'S ANALYSIS OF PROHAIRESIS (DELIBERATE CHOICE)

Having defined voluntary action, Aristotle now analyzes - the distinctively human capacity for rational choice that is most closely connected to virtue and character.

' ..
' ; . ' .

 Now that we have defined the voluntary and involuntary, the next topic to discuss is deliberate choice (prohairesis); for it seems to be most closely connected to virtue and to be a better criterion of character than actions are. Deliberate choice appears to be voluntary, but not the same thing - the voluntary is broader. For children and other animals share in the voluntary, but not in deliberate choice; and we call sudden actions voluntary but not chosen..
In general, deliberate choice seems to be concerned with things that are up to us (ta eph' hēmin)..
Is it then what has been previously deliberated about? For choice involves reason and thought. And the name itself seems to indicate that it is something chosen before (pro) other things.

Aristotle distinguishes prohairesis from.
- Appetite (ἐπιθυμία) - animals have it, choice opposes it in the continent person
- Spirited emotion (θυμός) - least of all seems chosen
- Wish (βούλησις) - can be for impossibles, choice cannot
- Belief (δόξα) - divided by true/false, choice by good/bad

The key insight: ' - choice concerns what is up to us.

Key concepts: deliberate choice, decision (prohairesis); appetite, desire (epithumia); spirited emotion, anger (thumos); wish (for ends) (boulēsis); belief, opinion (doxa).

record.text_content:
ARISTOTLE ON VOLUNTARINESS OF INTEMPERANCE VS COWARDICE

This chapter returns to the theme of voluntariness, arguing that intemperance is MORE voluntary than cowardice, which has implications for moral responsibility.

 Intemperance seems more like a voluntary thing than cowardice. For the one is because of pleasure, the other because of pain; and of these, pleasure is something chosen while pain is something avoided. Pain drives a person out of their nature and destroys it, but pleasure does nothing of the sort. So it is more voluntary. Hence it is also more disgraceful..
This chapter provides important clarification on degrees of voluntariness.
- Actions for pleasure are MORE voluntary than actions to avoid pain
- Pain can "drive us out of our nature" (ἐξίστησι) - an excuse
- Pleasure involves no such disruption - hence greater responsibility

This analysis becomes relevant for later debates about akrasia and compulsion.

Key concepts: voluntary (hekousion); intemperance (akolasia); cowardice (deilia); pleasure (chosen) (hēdonē); pain (avoided) (lupē); drives out, disturbs (existēsi).
